summary: Extends the IMAP URLFETCH command from URLAUTH so that third parties can get message parts in forms suited to non-mail applications. Previously the data was sent verbatim, which did not fit uses that need binary or converted content.

eli5.summary: A mail program can hand out a special link to part of a message. This note lets the receiver ask for that part in a more usable form, such as already decoded.

questions: how to fetch decoded message parts with imap urlauth
subtitle: Lets IMAP URLFETCH return decoded content and type metadata for a message part, not just the raw encoded bytes.

tldr.problem: The URLFETCH command from URLAUTH sends message part data verbatim, with no metadata to decode it, which does not suit applications that need the actual content.
tldr.mechanism: Each URL can be wrapped in parentheses with parameters BODYPARTSTRUCTURE, BINARY or BODY, and the server answers with matching metadata items, with BINARY having the content transfer encoding removed.
tldr.outcome: Servers advertise the extension with the URLAUTH=BINARY capability. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 5524 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 4467.

sections.title: The Problem with Verbatim Data
sections.content:
The URLFETCH command in IMAP URLAUTH (RFC 4467) dereferences a URL and returns the body-part data. It returns the encoded form, without enough metadata to decode it. That suits mail uses such as BURL (RFC 4468), where the encoded form is what is needed.

It does not suit uses that need the real content, such as streaming of message attachments. This memo adds a mechanism that returns extra metadata about the part, such as its media type, and removes any content transfer encoding that was applied.
sections.eli5: Asking for a message part used to be like getting a parcel still taped shut with no label. Now you can ask for it unwrapped and with a label saying what it is.

sections.title: Extended URLFETCH Parameters
sections.content:
The extension is available on a server that lists URLAUTH=BINARY in its capability string. A client uses it by enclosing each URL and its parameters in a parenthesized list. An unenclosed URL, or a list with no parameters, behaves exactly as in RFC 4467. An invalid URL also behaves as in RFC 4467 and returns a simple NIL.

Three parameters are defined:

  • BODYPARTSTRUCTURE asks for the structure as defined in the CONVERT extension (RFC 5259), which gives useful metadata such as the type of data.
  • BINARY asks for the data without any Content-Transfer-Encoding. The data MAY contain NUL octets, and then it MUST be sent using the literal8 syntax from the BINARY extension (RFC 3516).
  • BODY asks for the data as is, the same as unextended URLAUTH.

A metadata item MUST NOT appear more than once per URL, and a client MUST NOT request both BINARY and BODY.
sections.eli5: When you ask for a piece of a message, you can tick boxes: tell me what it is, give it to me unwrapped, or give it to me exactly as stored. You cannot tick both of the last two.

sections.title: Response Metadata
sections.content:
After the URL itself, the server includes a series of parenthesized metadata elements.

  • BODYPARTSTRUCTURE describes the data as returned, so it reflects any decoding done. If BINARY was also requested it shows an identity encoding. Unlike CONVERT, it is not given a part specifier, because the URL already implies it.
  • BINARY is the content with no transfer encoding applied. If that is not possible, for example because the server does not know the encoding, it MAY contain NIL. Servers MUST understand all identity content transfer encodings from MIME, plus Base64 and Quoted-Printable.
  • BODY is the content as found in the message, transfer encoding still applied. Asking only for it gives the same function as unextended URLAUTH.

The formal syntax says that content with a NUL octet MUST use literal8, other content SHOULD use nstring, and NIL is used on a decoding error.
sections.eli5: The answer comes back as labelled parts: a description of the item, the unwrapped item, or the original wrapped item. If the server cannot unwrap it, it says nothing for that part.

sections.title: Example Exchanges
sections.content:
The RFC gives several exchanges against a message in INBOX with uid=20.

  • Asking for BINARY on a text part returns the text as a plain literal, because it has no NUL octet.
  • Asking for BINARY BODYPARTSTRUCTURE on an image part returns a structure showing "IMAGE" "PNG" with encoding "BINARY" and size 123, then the data as a literal8 of 123 octets.
  • Asking for only BODYPARTSTRUCTURE returns the structure with the original "BASE64" encoding and size 164.
  • Asking for BINARY on a part with the unknown encoding X-BLURDYBLOOP returns the structure and (BINARY NIL).
  • Asking for a section that does not exist returns NIL in place of metadata.
sections.eli5: The examples show a friendly librarian handing over a book unwrapped, just its label, or the original wrapping, and saying plainly when a book cannot be unwrapped or is not on the shelf.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementors are directed to the security considerations of IMAP (RFC 3501), URLAUTH and BINARY. The new point is that whoever holds a URL can now fetch metadata about the content as well as the content, which could reveal more, including the original filename and a user-supplied description.

The RFC judges the extra value to an attacker as marginal. It applies only to URLs the attacker has no direct access to, such as those produced by URLAUTH, so implementors are again pointed to the URLAUTH considerations.
sections.eli5: A person holding the special link can now also learn what the item is called. That is a small extra clue, and the link already had to be given to them.
